l: Orange (fruit)
The orange, also called sweet orange to distinguish it from the <color=#3366CC>bitter orange</color> (<color=#3366CC>Citrus</color> × aurantium), is the <color=#3366CC>fruit</color> of a tree in
the <color=#3366CC>family</color> <color=#3366CC>Rutaceae</color>. Botanically, this is the hybrid Citrus × sinensis, between the <color=#3366CC>pomelo</color> (Citrus maxima) and the
<color=#3366CC>mandarin orange</color> (Citrus reticulata). The <color=#3366CC>chloroplast</color> <color=#3366CC>genome</color>, and therefore the maternal line, is that of pomelo. Hybrids
of the sweet orange form later types of mandarin and the <color=#3366CC>grapefruit</color>. The sweet orange has had its full <color=#3366CC>genome</color>
<color=#3366CC>sequenced</color>.
The orange originated in a region encompassing Southern China, <color=#3366CC>Northeast India</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color>; the earliest mention
of the sweet orange was in <color=#3366CC>Chinese literature</color> in 314 BC. Orange trees are widely grown in tropical and subtropical
areas for their sweet fruit. The fruit of the orange tree can be eaten fresh or processed for its juice or fragrant peel. In
2024, 67 million <color=#3366CC>tonnes</color> of oranges were grown worldwide, with <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color> producing 23% of the total, followed by <color=#3366CC>China</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>.
Oranges, variously understood, have featured in human culture since ancient times. They first appear in Western art in
the <color=#3366CC>Arnolfini Portrait</color> by <color=#3366CC>Jan van Eyck</color>, but they had been depicted in Chinese art centuries earlier, as in Zhao
Lingrang's <color=#3366CC>Song dynasty</color> fan painting Yellow Oranges and Green Tangerines. By the 17th century, an orangery had
become an item of prestige in Europe, as seen at the Versailles Orangerie. More recently, artists such as <color=#3366CC>Vincent van</color>
<color=#3366CC>Gogh</color>, John Sloan, and <color=#3366CC>Henri Matisse</color> included oranges in their paintings.
Description
The orange tree is a relatively small evergreen, <color=#3366CC>flowering</color> tree, with an average height of 9 to 10 m, although some very
old specimens can reach 15 m. Its oval <color=#3366CC>leaves</color>, which are alternately arranged, are 4 to 10 cm long and have crenulate
margins. Sweet oranges grow in a range of different sizes, and shapes varying from spherical to oblong. Inside and
attached to the rind is a porous white tissue, the white, bitter mesocarp or albedo (<color=#3366CC>pith</color>). The orange contains a number
of distinct <color=#3366CC>carpels</color> (segments or pigs, botanically the fruits) inside, typically about ten, each delimited by a membrane
and containing many juice-filled vesicles and usually a few <color=#3366CC>pips</color>. When unripe, the fruit is green. The grainy irregular
rind of the ripe fruit can range from bright orange to yellow-orange, but frequently retains green patches or, under warm
climate conditions, remains entirely green. Like all other citrus fruits, the sweet orange is non-climacteric, not ripening
off the tree. The Citrus sinensis group is subdivided into four classes with distinct characteristics: common oranges,
blood or pigmented oranges, navel oranges, and acidless oranges. The fruit is a hesperidium, a modified <color=#3366CC>berry</color>; it is
covered by a rind formed by a rugged thickening of the ovary wall.
History
Hybrid origins

<color=#3366CC>Citrus</color> trees are <color=#3366CC>angiosperms</color>, and most species are almost entirely <color=#3366CC>interfertile</color>. This includes <color=#3366CC>grapefruits</color>, <color=#3366CC>lemons</color>, <color=#3366CC>limes</color>,
oranges, and many citrus hybrids. As the interfertility of oranges and other citrus has produced numerous hybrids and
<color=#3366CC>cultivars</color>, and bud mutations have also been selected, citrus taxonomy has proven difficult.
The sweet orange, Citrus x sinensis, is not a wild fruit, but arose in <color=#3366CC>domestication</color> in East Asia. It originated in a region
encompassing Southern China, <color=#3366CC>Northeast India</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color>. The fruit was created as a cross between a non-pure
<color=#3366CC>mandarin orange</color> and a hybrid <color=#3366CC>pomelo</color> that had a substantial mandarin component. Since its <color=#3366CC>chloroplast DNA</color> is that of
pomelo, it was likely the hybrid pomelo, perhaps a pomelo BC1 backcross, that was the maternal parent of the first
orange. Based on genomic analysis, the relative proportions of the ancestral species in the sweet orange are
approximately 42% pomelo and 58% mandarin. All varieties of the sweet orange descend from this prototype cross,
differing only by mutations selected for during agricultural propagation. Sweet oranges have a distinct origin from the
bitter orange, which arose independently, perhaps in the wild, from a cross between pure mandarin and pomelo
parents.
Sweet oranges have in turn given rise to many further hybrids including the <color=#3366CC>grapefruit</color>, which arose from a sweet
orange x pomelo backcross. Spontaneous and engineered backcrosses between the sweet orange and mandarin
oranges or tangerines have produced the <color=#3366CC>clementine</color> and murcott. The ambersweet is a complex sweet orange x
(Orlando tangelo x clementine) hybrid. The citranges are a group of sweet orange x trifoliate orange (Citrus trifoliata)
hybrids.
Arab Agricultural Revolution
In Europe, the <color=#3366CC>Moors</color> introduced citrus fruits including the bitter orange, lemon, and lime to <color=#3366CC>al-Andalus</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Iberian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Peninsula</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Arab Agricultural Revolution</color>. Large-scale cultivation started in the 10th century, as evidenced by
complex irrigation techniques specifically adapted to support orange orchards. Citrus fruits—among them the bitter
orange—were introduced to Sicily in the 9th century during the period of the <color=#3366CC>Emirate of Sicily</color>, but the sweet orange
was unknown there until the late 15th century or the beginnings of the 16th century, when Italian and Portuguese
merchants brought orange trees into the Mediterranean area.
Spread across Europe
Shortly afterward, the sweet orange quickly was adopted as an edible fruit. It was considered a luxury food grown by
wealthy people in private conservatories, called <color=#3366CC>orangeries</color>. By 1646, the sweet orange was well known throughout
Europe; it went on to become the most often cultivated of all fruit trees. <color=#3366CC>Louis XIV</color> of France had a great love of orange
trees and built the grandest of all royal Orangeries at the <color=#3366CC>Palace of Versailles</color>. At Versailles, potted orange trees in solid
silver tubs were placed throughout the rooms of the palace, while the Orangerie allowed year-round cultivation of the
fruit to supply the court. When Louis condemned his finance minister, Nicolas Fouquet, in 1664, part of the treasures
that he confiscated were over 1,000 orange trees from Fouquet's estate at Vaux-le-Vicomte.
To the Americas
Spanish travellers introduced the sweet orange to the American continent. On his second voyage in 1493, <color=#3366CC>Christopher</color>
<color=#3366CC>Columbus</color> may have planted the fruit on <color=#3366CC>Hispaniola</color>. Subsequent expeditions in the mid-1500s brought sweet oranges
to South America and Mexico, and to Florida in 1565, when Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded <color=#3366CC>St Augustine</color>. Spanish
missionaries brought orange trees to Arizona between 1707 and 1710, while the Franciscans did the same in San
Diego, California, in 1769. Archibald Menzies, the botanist on the Vancouver Expedition, collected orange seeds in
South Africa, raised the seedlings on board, and gave them to several Hawaiian chiefs in 1792. The sweet orange
came to be grown across the <color=#3366CC>Hawaiian Islands</color>, but its cultivation stopped after the arrival of the Mediterranean fruit fly
in the early 1900s. <color=#3366CC>Florida</color> farmers obtained seeds from New Orleans around 1872, after which orange groves were
established by grafting the sweet orange on to sour orange rootstocks.
California
Citrus cultivation in California began with the Spanish missionaries, who planted oranges and lemons at <color=#3366CC>Baja California</color>
around 1739 and at Alta California missions by 1769. Early fruit was thick-skinned and sour, not suited for commercial
markets. The first sizeable grove was established at Mission San Gabriel in 1804, with about 400 trees on six acres.
This mission-based agriculture ended with secularisation which closed the missions and gave away their lands in 1835.
Jean-Louis Vignes likely planted the first private orange grove in Los Angeles in 1834. William Wolfskill planted his
orchard in Los Angeles in 1841. By 1862, his orchards held two-thirds of the state's orange trees. The <color=#3366CC>California gold</color>
<color=#3366CC>rush</color> (from 1849) increased demand for oranges, especially for their <color=#3366CC>vitamin C</color>, which helped prevent <color=#3366CC>scurvy</color> among
miners. This spurred gradual expansion of orchards. In the early 1870s, Wolfskill's reported profits of $1,000 per acre
attracted Midwestern farmers to citrus growing, especially in Orange County.
The 1870s saw the introduction of improved fruit varieties. In 1873, navel orange plants from Brazil were distributed by
the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Luther C. Tibbets and Eliza Tibbets successfully cultivated these in Riverside,
leading to widespread planting of the sweet, seedless navel orange, which became the backbone of the California
citrus industry. The Valencia orange, introduced in 1876, matured in summer and fall, complementing the
winter-ripening navel and providing oranges year-round. The completion of major railroads (Southern Pacific in 1877,
and the Santa Fe in 1885) and the introduction of ventilated boxcars revolutionised distribution, opening national
markets and triggering a planting frenzy in southern California. By 1885, the number of citrus trees in California had
grown from 90,000 (in 1875) to 2 million, and to 4.5 million by 1901.
The 1890s brought pest control advances (spraying, fumigation) and frost protection (heaters, later wind machines).
The University of California established its Citrus Experiment Station in 1907, supporting research and innovation.
Cooperative marketing emerged with the formation of the California Fruit Growers Exchange in 1905, later known as
Sunkist Growers Inc., which helped standardise and market California citrus worldwide. By the 1980s, California was
the second largest orange producer in the U.S., after Florida.
Etymology
The word "orange" has its <color=#3366CC>etymological</color> roots in the <color=#3366CC>Dravidian language family</color> of South India. From there, the word
passed to <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color> (nāranga), meaning 'orange tree'. The Sanskrit word reached European languages through <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>
(nārang) and its <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> derivative (nāranj). The word entered <color=#3366CC>Late Middle English</color> in the 14th century via <color=#3366CC>Old French</color>
pomme d'orenge. Other forms include Old Provençal auranja, Italian arancia, formerly narancia. In several languages,
the initial n present in earlier forms of the word dropped off because it may have been mistaken as part of an indefinite
article ending in an n sound. In French, for example, une norenge may have been heard as une orenge. This linguistic
change is called juncture loss. <color=#3366CC>The colour</color> was named after the fruit, with the first recorded use of orange as a colour
name in English in 1512.
Composition
Nutrition
Orange flesh is 87% water, 12% <color=#3366CC>carbohydrates</color>, 1% <color=#3366CC>protein</color>, and contains negligible <color=#3366CC>fat</color> (table). In a reference amount
of 100 g, orange flesh provides 47 <color=#3366CC>calories</color>, and is a rich source of <color=#3366CC>vitamin C</color>, providing 59% of the Daily Value, with no
other micronutrients in significant amounts (table).
Phytochemicals
Oranges contain diverse phytochemicals, including <color=#3366CC>carotenoids</color> (<color=#3366CC>beta-carotene</color>, <color=#3366CC>lutein</color> and beta-cryptoxanthin),

<color=#3366CC>flavonoids</color> (e.g. naringenin) and numerous <color=#3366CC>volatile organic compounds</color> producing orange <color=#3366CC>aroma</color>, including <color=#3366CC>aldehydes</color>,

<color=#3366CC>esters</color>, <color=#3366CC>terpenes</color>, <color=#3366CC>alcohols</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ketones</color>. Orange juice contains only about one-fifth the <color=#3366CC>citric acid</color> of <color=#3366CC>lime</color> or <color=#3366CC>lemon</color> juice
(which contain about 47 g/L).
Taste
The taste of oranges is determined mainly by the ratio of sugars to acids, whereas orange aroma derives from <color=#3366CC>volatile</color>

<color=#3366CC>organic compounds</color>, including <color=#3366CC>alcohols</color>, <color=#3366CC>aldehydes</color>, <color=#3366CC>ketones</color>, <color=#3366CC>terpenes</color>, and <color=#3366CC>esters</color>. Bitter limonoid compounds, such as
limonin, decrease gradually during development, whereas volatile aroma compounds tend to peak in mid- to
late-season development. Taste quality tends to improve later in harvests when there is a higher sugar/acid ratio with
less bitterness. As a citrus fruit, the orange is acidic, with <color=#3366CC>pH</color> levels ranging from 2.9 to 4.0. Taste and aroma vary
according to genetic background, environmental conditions during development, ripeness at harvest, postharvest
conditions, and storage duration.
Cultivars
Common
Common oranges (also called "white", "round", or "blond" oranges) constitute about two-thirds of all orange production.
The majority of this crop is used for juice.
Valencia
The Valencia orange is a late-season fruit; it is popular when navel oranges are out of season. Thomas Rivers, an
English nurseryman, imported this variety from the <color=#3366CC>Azores</color> and catalogued it in 1865 under the name Excelsior. Around
1870, he provided trees to S. B. Parsons, a <color=#3366CC>Long Island</color> nurseryman, who in turn sold them to E. H. Hart of Federal
Point, Florida.
Navel
Navel oranges have a characteristic second fruit at the <color=#3366CC>apex</color>, which protrudes slightly like a human <color=#3366CC>navel</color>. They are
mainly an eating fruit, as their thicker skin makes them easy to peel, they are less juicy and their bitterness makes them
less suitable for juice. The parent variety was probably the Portuguese navel orange or Umbigo. The cultivar rapidly
spread to other countries, but being seedless it had to be propagated by cutting and <color=#3366CC>grafting</color>.
The Cara Cara is a type of navel orange grown mainly in <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Africa</color> and California's San Joaquin Valley.
It is sweet and low in acid, with distinctively pinkish red flesh. It was discovered at the Hacienda Cara Cara in <color=#3366CC>Valencia</color>,
Venezuela, in 1976.
Blood
Blood oranges, with an intense red colouration inside, are widely grown around the Mediterranean; there are several
cultivars. The development of the red colour requires cool nights. The redness is mainly due to the <color=#3366CC>anthocyanin</color>
pigment chrysanthemin (cyanidin 3-O-glucoside).
Acidless
Acidless oranges are an early-season fruit with very low levels of acid. They also are called "sweet" oranges in the
United States, with similar names in other countries: douce in France, sucrena in Spain, dolce or maltese in Italy, meski
in North Africa and the Near East (where they are especially popular), succari in Egypt, and lima in Brazil. The lack of
acid, which protects orange juice against spoilage in other groups, renders them generally unfit for processing as juice,
so they are primarily eaten. They remain profitable in areas of local consumption, but rapid spoilage renders them
unsuitable for export to major population centres of Europe, Asia, or the United States.
Cultivation
Climate
Like most citrus plants, oranges do well under moderate temperatures—between 15.5 and 29 C—and require
considerable amounts of sunshine and water. They are principally grown in tropical and subtropical regions.
As oranges are sensitive to <color=#3366CC>frost</color>, farmers have developed methods to protect the trees from frost damage. A common
process is to spray the trees with water so as to cover them with a thin layer of ice, insulating them even if air
temperatures drop far lower. This practice, however, offers protection only for a very short time. Another procedure
involves burning fuel oil in <color=#3366CC>smudge pots</color> put between the trees. These burn with a great deal of particulate emission, so
condensation of water vapour on the particulate soot prevents condensation on plants and raises the air temperature
very slightly. Smudge pots were developed after a disastrous freeze in southern California in January 1913 destroyed a
whole crop.
Propagation

Commercially grown orange trees are <color=#3366CC>propagated</color> <color=#3366CC>asexually</color> by <color=#3366CC>grafting</color> a mature <color=#3366CC>cultivar</color> onto a suitable <color=#3366CC>seedling</color>
rootstock to ensure the same <color=#3366CC>yield</color>, identical fruit characteristics, and resistance to diseases throughout the years.
Propagation involves two stages: first, a rootstock is grown from seed. Then, when it is approximately one year old, the
leafy top is cut off and a <color=#3366CC>bud</color> taken from a specific <color=#3366CC>scion</color> variety, is grafted into its bark. The scion is what determines
the variety of orange, while the rootstock makes the tree resistant to pests and diseases and adaptable to specific <color=#3366CC>soil</color>
and climatic conditions. Thus, rootstocks influence the rate of growth and have an effect on fruit yield and quality.
Rootstocks must be compatible with the variety inserted into them because otherwise, the tree may decline, be less
productive, or die. Among the advantages to grafting are that trees mature uniformly and begin to bear fruit earlier than
those reproduced by seeds (3 to 4 years in contrast with 6 to 7 years), and that farmers can combine the best attributes
of a scion with those of a rootstock.
Harvest
Canopy-shaking mechanical harvesters are being used increasingly in Florida to harvest oranges. Current canopy
shaker machines use a series of six-to-seven-foot-long tines to shake the tree canopy at a relatively constant stroke
and frequency. Oranges are picked once they are pale orange.
Degreening
Oranges must be mature when harvested. In the United States, laws forbid harvesting immature fruit for human
consumption in Texas, Arizona, California, and Florida. Ripe oranges, however, often have some green or yellow-green
colour in the skin. <color=#3366CC>Ethylene</color> gas is used to turn green skin to orange. This process is known as "degreening", "gassing",
"sweating", or "curing". Oranges are non-climacteric fruits, and cannot ripen internally in response to ethylene gas after
harvesting, though they will de-green externally.
Storage
Commercially, oranges can be stored by refrigeration in controlled-atmosphere chambers for up to twelve weeks after
harvest. Storage life ultimately depends on cultivar, maturity, pre-harvest conditions, and handling. At home, oranges
have a shelf life of about one month, and are best stored loose.
Pests and diseases
Pests
The first major pest that attacked orange trees in the United States was the cottony cushion scale (Icerya purchasi),
imported from Australia to California in 1868. Within 20 years, it wiped out the citrus orchards around Los Angeles, and
limited orange growth throughout California. In 1888, the USDA sent Alfred Koebele to Australia to study this <color=#3366CC>scale</color>
<color=#3366CC>insect</color> in its native habitat. He brought back with him specimens of an Australian <color=#3366CC>ladybird</color>, Novius cardinalis (the Vedalia
beetle), and within a decade the pest was controlled. This was one of the first successful applications of <color=#3366CC>biological pest</color>
<color=#3366CC>control</color> on any crop. The orange dog caterpillar of the giant swallowtail butterfly, Papilio cresphontes, is a pest of citrus
plantations in North America, where it eats new foliage and can defoliate young trees.
Diseases
Citrus greening disease, caused by the bacterium Liberobacter asiaticum, has been the most serious threat to orange
production since 2010. It is characterised by streaks of different shades on the leaves, and deformed, poorly coloured,
unsavoury fruit. In areas where the disease is endemic, citrus trees live for only five to eight years and never bear fruit
suitable for consumption. In the western hemisphere, the disease was discovered in Florida in 1998, where it has
attacked nearly all the trees ever since. It was reported in Brazil by Fundecitrus Brasil in 2004. As from 2009, 0.87% of
the trees in Brazil's main orange growing areas (São Paulo and Minas Gerais) showed symptoms of greening, an
increase of 49% over 2008. The disease is spread primarily by psyllid plant lice such as the Asian citrus psyllid
(Diaphorina citri Kuwayama), an efficient <color=#3366CC>vector</color> of the bacterium. Foliar <color=#3366CC>insecticides</color> reduce psyllid populations for a
short time, but also suppress beneficial predatory ladybird beetles. Soil application of aldicarb provided limited control
of Asian citrus psyllid, while drenches of imidacloprid to young trees were effective for two months or more.
Management of citrus greening disease requires an integrated approach that includes use of clean stock, elimination of
inoculum via voluntary and regulatory means, use of pesticides to control psyllid vectors in the citrus crop, and
biological control of the vectors in non-crop reservoirs.
Greasy spot, a fungal disease caused by the ascomycete Mycosphaerella citri, produces leaf spots and premature
defoliation, thus reducing the tree's vigour and yield. Ascospores of M. citri are generated in pseudothecia in
decomposing fallen leaves.
Production
In 2024, world production of oranges was 67 million <color=#3366CC>tonnes</color>, led by Brazil with 23% of the total, followed by China,
Mexico, and Egypt (table).
Culinary use
Dessert fruit and juice
Oranges, whose flavour may vary from <color=#3366CC>sweet</color> to sour, are commonly peeled and eaten fresh raw as a dessert. <color=#3366CC>Orange</color>
<color=#3366CC>juice</color> is obtained by squeezing the fruit on a special tool (a juicer or squeezer) and collecting the juice in a tray or tank
underneath. This can be made at home or, on a much larger scale, industrially. Orange juice is a traded commodity on
the Intercontinental Exchange. Frozen orange juice concentrate is made from freshly squeezed and filtered juice.
Marmalade
Oranges are made into <color=#3366CC>jam</color> in many countries; in Britain, bitter <color=#3366CC>Seville oranges</color> are used to make <color=#3366CC>marmalade</color>. Almost
the whole Spanish production is exported to Britain for this purpose. The entire fruit is cut up and boiled with sugar; the
pith contributes <color=#3366CC>pectin</color>, which helps the marmalade to set. The first recipe was by an Englishwoman, Mary Kettilby, in
1714. Pieces of peel were first added by Janet Keiller of <color=#3366CC>Dundee</color> in the 1790s, contributing a distinctively bitter taste.
Orange peel contains the bitter substances <color=#3366CC>limonene</color> and naringin.
Extracts
Zest is scraped from the coloured outer part of the peel, and used as a flavouring and garnish in desserts and <color=#3366CC>cocktails</color>.
Sweet orange oil is a <color=#3366CC>by-product</color> of the juice industry produced by pressing the peel. It is used for flavouring food and
drinks; it is employed in the perfume industry and in aromatherapy for its <color=#3366CC>fragrance</color>. The oil consists of approximately
90% D-limonene, a <color=#3366CC>solvent</color> used in household chemicals such as wood conditioners for furniture and—along with other
citrus oils—detergents and hand cleansers. It is an efficient cleaning agent with a pleasant smell, promoted for being
environmentally friendly and therefore preferable to petrochemicals. It is, however, irritating to the skin and toxic to
aquatic life.
In culture
Oranges have featured in human culture since ancient times. The earliest mention of the sweet orange in <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>
<color=#3366CC>literature</color> dates from 314 BC. Larissa Pham, in The Paris Review, notes that sweet oranges were available in China
much earlier than in the West. She writes that Zhao Lingrang's fan painting Yellow Oranges and Green Tangerines
pays attention not to the fruit's colour but the shape of the fruit-laden trees, and that <color=#3366CC>Su Shi</color>'s poem on the same subject
runs "You must remember, / the best scenery of the year, / Is exactly now, / when oranges turn yellow and tangerines
green."
The scholar Cristina Mazzoni has examined the multiple uses of the fruit in Italian art and literature, from <color=#3366CC>Catherine of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Siena</color>'s sending of candied oranges to Pope Urban, to <color=#3366CC>Sandro Botticelli</color>'s setting of his painting <color=#3366CC>Primavera</color> in an orange
grove. She notes that oranges symbolised desire and wealth on the one hand, and deformity on the other, while in the
fairy-stories of Sicily, they have magical properties. Pham comments that the <color=#3366CC>Arnolfini Portrait</color> by <color=#3366CC>Jan van Eyck</color> contains
in a small detail one of the first representations of oranges in Western art, the costly fruit perhaps traded by the
merchant Arnolfini himself. By the 17th century, <color=#3366CC>orangeries</color> were added to great houses in Europe, both to enable the
fruit to be grown locally and for prestige, as seen in the Versailles Orangerie completed in 1686.
The Dutch <color=#3366CC>Post-Impressionist</color> artist <color=#3366CC>Vincent van Gogh</color> portrayed oranges in paintings such as his 1889 Still Life of
Oranges and Lemons with Blue Gloves and his 1890 A Child with Orange, both works late in his life. The American
artist of the Ashcan School, John Sloan, made a 1935 painting Blond Nude with Orange, Blue Couch, while <color=#3366CC>Henri</color>
<color=#3366CC>Matisse</color>'s last painting was his 1951 Nude with Oranges; after that he only made cut-outs.
Andes
The Andes, Andes Mountains or Andean Mountain Range (Spanish: Cordillera de los Andes; Anti) are the longest
continental mountain range in the world, forming a continuous <color=#3366CC>highland</color> along the western edge of <color=#3366CC>South America</color>. The
range is 8900 km long and 200 to 700 km wide (widest between 18°S and 20°S <color=#3366CC>latitude</color>) and has an average height of
about 4000 m. The Andes extend from south to north through seven South American countries: <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Bolivia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Peru</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>, <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>.
Along their length, the Andes are split into several ranges, separated by intermediate <color=#3366CC>depressions</color>. The Andes are the

location of several high <color=#3366CC>plateaus</color>—some of which host major cities such as <color=#3366CC>Arequipa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bogotá</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cali</color>, <color=#3366CC>Medellín</color>, El Alto, <color=#3366CC>La</color>

<color=#3366CC>Paz</color>, Mérida, <color=#3366CC>Santiago</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sucre</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Altiplano Plateau</color> is the world's second highest after the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Plateau</color>. These
ranges are in turn grouped into three major divisions based on climate: the Tropical Andes, the Dry Andes, and the Wet
Andes.
The Andes are the highest mountain range outside of <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>. The range's highest peak, Argentina's <color=#3366CC>Aconcagua</color>, rises to
an elevation of about 6961 m above sea level. The peak of <color=#3366CC>Chimborazo</color> in the Ecuadorian Andes is farther from the
Earth's center than any other location on the Earth's surface, due to the <color=#3366CC>equatorial bulge</color> resulting from the <color=#3366CC>Earth's</color>
<color=#3366CC>rotation</color>. The world's highest <color=#3366CC>volcanoes</color> are in the Andes, including <color=#3366CC>Ojos del Salado</color> on the Chile–Argentina border,
which rises to 6893 m.
The Andes are also part of the <color=#3366CC>American Cordillera</color>, a chain of mountain ranges (cordillera) that consists of an almost
continuous sequence of mountain ranges that form the western "backbone" of the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>.
Etymology
The <color=#3366CC>etymology</color> of the word Andes has been debated. The majority consensus is that it derives from the <color=#3366CC>Quechua</color> word
anti "east" as in Antisuyu (Quechua for "east region"), one of the four regions of the <color=#3366CC>Inca Empire</color>. Others suggest that it
is in fact from the word anta (meaning copper) of the older <color=#3366CC>Aymara language</color>.
The term cordillera comes from the <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> word cordel "rope" and is used as a descriptive name for several
contiguous sections of the Andes, as well as the entire Andean range, and the combined mountain chain along the
western part of the North and South American <color=#3366CC>continents</color>.
Geography
The Andes mountain range, the longest continental mountain system in the world, extends approximately 7000 km
along the western edge of <color=#3366CC>South America</color>, spanning seven countries. Its width varies from 200 km to 700 km,
encompassing a series of parallel cordilleras, high plateaus, and deep intermontane valleys. Prominent peaks such as
<color=#3366CC>Aconcagua</color> at 6961 m in Argentina, Huascarán at 6768 m in Peru, and <color=#3366CC>Illimani</color> 6438 m in Bolivia illustrate the extreme
elevations and rugged relief that define the range. The Andes encompass a wide variety of climatic and <color=#3366CC>ecological</color>
zones, ranging from humid cloud forests on the eastern slopes to the arid high plains of the <color=#3366CC>Altiplano</color> and the glaciated
summits of the southern Andes. These sharp environmental gradients have strongly influenced human settlement and
the development of major highland cities such as Bogotá, Cusco, La Paz and Quito.
The Andes can be divided into three sections:
• The Southern Andes in <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> and <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, south of <color=#3366CC>Llullaillaco</color>;
• The Central Andes in <color=#3366CC>Bolivia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Peru</color>; and
• The Northern Andes in <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>. The northern Andes are separated into three
branches.
At the northern end of the Andes, the separate Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta range is often, but not always, treated as
part of the Northern Andes.

The <color=#3366CC>Leeward Antilles</color> islands <color=#3366CC>Aruba</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bonaire</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Curaçao</color>, which lie in the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Sea</color> off the coast of <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>,
were formerly thought to represent the submerged peaks of the extreme northern edge of the Andes range, but
ongoing geological studies indicate that such a simplification does not do justice to the complex tectonic boundary
between the <color=#3366CC>South American</color> and <color=#3366CC>Caribbean plates</color>.
Geology
The Andes are an <color=#3366CC>orogenic</color> belt of mountains along the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ring of Fire</color>, a zone of <color=#3366CC>volcanic activity</color> that
encompasses the Pacific rim of the Americas as well as the Asia-Pacific region. The Andes are the result of <color=#3366CC>tectonic</color>

<color=#3366CC>plate</color> processes extending during the <color=#3366CC>Mesozoic</color> and Tertiary eras, caused by the <color=#3366CC>subduction</color> of <color=#3366CC>oceanic crust</color> beneath
the <color=#3366CC>South American Plate</color> as the <color=#3366CC>Nazca Plate</color> and South American Plate converge. These processes were accelerated
by the effects of climate. As the uplift of the Andes created a rain shadow on the western fringes of <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, <color=#3366CC>ocean</color>
<color=#3366CC>currents</color> and prevailing winds carried moisture away from the Chilean coast. This caused some areas of the subduction
zone to be sediment-starved, which in turn prevented the subducting plate from having a well lubricated surface. These
factors increased the rate of contractional coastal uplift in the Andes. The main cause of the rise of the Andes is the
contraction of the western rim of the <color=#3366CC>South American Plate</color> due to the subduction of the <color=#3366CC>Nazca Plate</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Plate</color>. To the east, the Andes range is bounded by several <color=#3366CC>sedimentary basins</color>, such as the Orinoco Basin, the Amazon
Basin, the Madre de Dios Basin, and the <color=#3366CC>Gran Chaco</color>, that separate the Andes from the ancient <color=#3366CC>cratons</color> in eastern
South America. In the south, the Andes share a long boundary with the former <color=#3366CC>Patagonia Terrane</color>. To the west, the
Andes end at the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>, although the Peru–Chile Trench can be considered their ultimate western limit. The
Andean orogen has a series of bends or oroclines. The Bolivian Orocline is a seaward-concave bending in the coast of
<color=#3366CC>South America</color> and the Andes Mountains at about 18° S. At this point, the orientation of the Andes turns from northwest
in <color=#3366CC>Peru</color> to south in <color=#3366CC>Chile</color> and <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>. The Andean segments north and south of the Orocline have been rotated 15°
counter-clockwise to 20° clockwise respectively. The Bolivian Orocline area overlaps with the area of the maximum
width of the <color=#3366CC>Altiplano Plateau</color>, and according to Isacks (1988) the Orocline is related to crustal shortening. The specific
point at 18° S where the <color=#3366CC>coastline</color> bends is known as the <color=#3366CC>Arica</color> Elbow. Further south lies the Maipo Orocline, a more
subtle orocline between 30° S and 38°S with a seaward-concave break in the trend at 33° S. Near the southern tip of
the Andes lies the Patagonian Orocline.
Orogeny
The western rim of the <color=#3366CC>South American Plate</color> has been the place of several pre-Andean <color=#3366CC>orogenies</color> since at least the
late <color=#3366CC>Proterozoic</color> and early <color=#3366CC>Paleozoic</color>, when several terranes and <color=#3366CC>microcontinents</color> collided and amalgamated with the
ancient <color=#3366CC>cratons</color> of eastern South America, by then the South American part of <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>.
The formation of the modern Andes began with the events of the <color=#3366CC>Triassic</color>, when <color=#3366CC>Pangaea</color> began the breakup that
resulted in developing several <color=#3366CC>rifts</color>. The development continued through the <color=#3366CC>Jurassic</color> Period. It was during the

<color=#3366CC>Cretaceous</color> Period that the Andes began to take their present form, by the <color=#3366CC>uplifting</color>, <color=#3366CC>faulting</color>, and <color=#3366CC>folding</color> of <color=#3366CC>sedimentary</color>
and <color=#3366CC>metamorphic</color> rocks of the ancient cratons to the east. The rise of the Andes has not been constant, as different
regions have had different degrees of tectonic stress, uplift, and <color=#3366CC>erosion</color>.
Across the 1000 km <color=#3366CC>Drake Passage</color> lie the mountains of the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Peninsula</color> south of the <color=#3366CC>Scotia Plate</color>, which
appear to be a continuation of the Andes chain.
The far east regions of the Andes experience a series of changes resulting from the Andean orogeny. Parts of the
Sunsás Orogen in Amazonian craton disappeared from the surface of the earth, being <color=#3366CC>overridden</color> by the Andes. The
Sierras de Córdoba, where the effects of the ancient Pampean orogeny can be observed, owe their modern uplift and
relief to the <color=#3366CC>Andean orogeny</color> in the Tertiary. Further south in southern <color=#3366CC>Patagonia</color>, the onset of the Andean orogeny
caused the Magallanes Basin to evolve from being an extensional <color=#3366CC>back-arc basin</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Mesozoic</color> to being a
contractional foreland basin in the <color=#3366CC>Cenozoic</color>.
Seismic activity
Tectonic forces above the <color=#3366CC>subduction zone</color> along the entire west coast of South America where the <color=#3366CC>Nazca Plate</color> and a
part of the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Plate</color> are sliding beneath the <color=#3366CC>South American Plate</color> continue to produce an ongoing <color=#3366CC>orogenic event</color>
resulting in minor to major <color=#3366CC>earthquakes</color> and volcanic eruptions to this day. Many high-magnitude earthquakes have
been recorded in the region, such as the 2010 Maule earthquake (M8.8), the 2015 Illapel earthquake (M8.2), and the
<color=#3366CC>1960 Valdivia earthquake</color> (M9.5), which as of 2024 was the strongest ever recorded on seismometers.
The amount, magnitude, and type of seismic activity varies greatly along the subduction zone. These differences are
due to a wide range of factors, including friction between the plates, angle of subduction, buoyancy of the subducting
plate, rate of subduction, and hydration value of the mantle material. The highest rate of seismic activity is observed in
the central portion of the boundary, between 33°S and 35°S. In this area, the angle of subduction is very low, meaning
the subducting plate is nearly horizontal. Studies of mantle hydration across the subduction zone have shown a
correlation between increased material hydration and lower-magnitude, more frequent seismic activity. Zones exhibiting
dehydration instead are thought to have a higher potential for larger, high-magnitude earthquakes in the future.
The mountain range is also a source of shallow intraplate earthquakes within the South American Plate. The largest
such earthquake (as of 2024) struck Peru in 1947 and measured 7.5. In the Peruvian Andes, these earthquakes display
normal (1946), strike-slip (1976), and reverse (1969, 1983) mechanisms. The Amazonian Craton is actively
underthrusted beneath the sub-Andes region of Peru, producing thrust faults. In Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, thrust
faulting occurs along the sub-Andes due in response to contraction brought on by subduction, while in the high Andes,
normal faulting occurs in response to gravitational forces.
In the extreme south, a major <color=#3366CC>transform fault</color> separates <color=#3366CC>Tierra del Fuego</color> from the small <color=#3366CC>Scotia Plate</color>.
Volcanism
The Andes range has many active volcanoes distributed in four volcanic zones separated by areas of inactivity. The
Andean volcanism is a result of the <color=#3366CC>subduction</color> of the Nazca Plate and Antarctic Plate underneath the South American
Plate. The belt is subdivided into four main volcanic zones that are separated from each other by volcanic gaps. The
volcanoes of the belt are diverse in terms of activity style, products, and morphology. Although some differences can be
explained by which volcanic zone a volcano belongs to, there are significant differences inside volcanic zones and even
between neighboring volcanoes. Despite being a typical location for calc-alkalic and subduction volcanism, the Andean
Volcanic Belt has a large range of volcano-tectonic settings, such as rift systems, extensional zones, transpressional
faults, subduction of <color=#3366CC>mid-ocean ridges</color>, and <color=#3366CC>seamount</color> chains apart from a large range of crustal thicknesses and
<color=#3366CC>magma</color> ascent paths, and different amount of crustal assimilations.
Ore deposits and evaporites
The Andes Mountains host large <color=#3366CC>ore</color> and <color=#3366CC>salt</color> deposits, and some of their eastern fold and thrust belts act as traps for
commercially exploitable amounts of <color=#3366CC>hydrocarbons</color>. In the forelands of the <color=#3366CC>Atacama Desert</color>, some of the largest
<color=#3366CC>porphyry copper</color> mineralizations occur, making Chile and Peru the first- and second-largest exporters of <color=#3366CC>copper</color> in the
world. Porphyry copper in the western slopes of the Andes has been generated by hydrothermal fluids (mostly water)
during the cooling of <color=#3366CC>plutons</color> or volcanic systems. The porphyry mineralization further benefited from the dry climate
that reduced the disturbing actions of meteoric water. The dry climate in the central western Andes has also led to the
creation of extensive saltpeter deposits that were extensively mined until the invention of synthetic <color=#3366CC>nitrates</color>. Yet another
result of the dry climate are the <color=#3366CC>salars</color> of Atacama and Uyuni, the former being the largest source of <color=#3366CC>lithium</color> and the
latter the world's largest reserve of the element. Early Mesozoic and <color=#3366CC>Neogene</color> plutonism in Bolivia's Cordillera Central
created the Bolivian tin belt as well as the famous, now mostly depleted, silver deposits of Cerro Rico de Potosí.
Climate
The Andes Mountains is connected to the climate of South America, particularly through the hyper-arid conditions of
the adjacent <color=#3366CC>Atacama Desert</color>. The Atacama Bench, a prominent low-relief feature along the Pacific seaboard, serves
as a key geomorphological record of the long-term interplay between Andean tectonics and Cenozoic climate. While
the initial uplift and shortening of the Andes were driven by the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South
American Plate, arid climate acted as an important feedback mechanism. Reduced erosion rates in the increasingly
arid Atacama region may have effectively stopped tectonic activity in certain parts of the mountain range. This lack of
erosion could have facilitated the eastward propagation of deformation, leading to the widening of the Andean orogen
over time. Thus, the Atacama Desert and its geological features, like the Atacama Bench, offer critical insights into the
coupled evolution of the Andes Mountains and the changing regional climate.
History
The Andes Mountains, initially inhabited by <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherers</color>, experienced the development of <color=#3366CC>agriculture</color> and the rise
of politically centralized <color=#3366CC>civilizations</color>, which culminated in the establishment of the century-long <color=#3366CC>Inca Empire</color>. This all
changed in the 16th century, when the Spanish conquistadors colonized the mountains in advance of the <color=#3366CC>mining</color>
economy.
In the tide of anti-imperialist nationalism, the Andes became the scene of a <color=#3366CC>series of independence wars</color> in the 19th
century, when rebel forces swept through the region to overthrow <color=#3366CC>Spanish colonial</color> rule. Since then, many former
Spanish territories have become five independent Andean states.
Climate and hydrology
The climate in the Andes varies greatly depending on latitude, altitude, and proximity to the sea. Temperature,
atmospheric pressure, and humidity decrease in higher elevations. The southern section is rainy and cool, while the
central section is dry. The northern Andes are typically rainy and warm, with an average temperature of 18 C in
<color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>. The climate is known to change drastically in rather short distances. <color=#3366CC>Rainforests</color> exist just kilometers away
from the snow-covered peak of <color=#3366CC>Cotopaxi</color>. The mountains have a large effect on the temperatures of nearby areas. The
snow line depends on the location. It is between 4500 and 4800 m in the tropical Ecuadorian, Colombian, Venezuelan,
and northern Peruvian Andes, rising to 4800 – 5200 m in the drier mountains of southern Peru and northern Chile south
to about 30°S before descending to 4500 m on Aconcagua at 32°S, 2000 m at 40°S, 500 m at 50°S, and only 300 m in
<color=#3366CC>Tierra del Fuego</color> at 55°S; from 50°S, several of the larger glaciers descend to sea level.
The Andes of Chile and <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> can be divided into two climatic and glaciological zones: the Dry Andes and the Wet
Andes. Since the Dry Andes extend from the latitudes of the <color=#3366CC>Atacama Desert</color> to the area of the Maule River,
precipitation is more sporadic, and there are strong temperature oscillations. The line of equilibrium may shift drastically
over short periods of time, leaving a whole glacier in the ablation area or in the accumulation area.
In the high Andes of Central Chile and <color=#3366CC>Mendoza Province</color>, rock glaciers are larger and more common than glaciers;
this is due to the high exposure to <color=#3366CC>solar radiation</color>. In these regions, glaciers occur typically at higher altitudes than rock
glaciers. The lowest active rock glaciers occur at 900 m a.s.l. in <color=#3366CC>Aconcagua</color>.
Though precipitation increases with height, there are semiarid conditions in the nearly 7000. m highest mountains of
the Andes. This dry <color=#3366CC>steppe</color> climate is considered to be typical of the subtropical position at 32–34° S. The valley
bottoms have no woods, just dwarf scrub. The largest glaciers, for example the Plomo Glacier and the Horcones
Glaciers, do not even reach 10 km in length and have only insignificant ice thickness. At glacial times, however, c.
20,000 years ago, the glaciers were over ten times longer. On the east side of this section of the Mendozina Andes,
they flowed down to 2060 m and on the west side to about 1220 m above sea level. The massifs of <color=#3366CC>Aconcagua</color> (6961
m), Tupungato (6550 m), and Nevado Juncal (6110 m) are tens of kilometres away from each other and were
connected by a joint ice stream network. The Andes' dendritic glacier arms, components of valley glaciers, were up to
112.5 km long and over 1250 m thick, and spanned a vertical distance of 5150 m. The climatic glacier snowline (ELA)
was lowered from 4600 m to 3200 m at glacial times.
Flora
The Andean region cuts across several natural and floristic regions, due to its extension, from <color=#3366CC>Caribbean</color> Venezuela to

cold, windy, and wet <color=#3366CC>Cape Horn</color> passing through the hyperarid <color=#3366CC>Atacama Desert</color>. <color=#3366CC>Rainforests</color> and <color=#3366CC>tropical dry forests</color>
used to encircle much of the northern Andes but are now greatly <color=#3366CC>diminished</color>, especially in the Chocó and inter-Andean
valleys of Colombia. Opposite the humid Andean slopes are the relatively dry Andean slopes in most of western Peru,
Chile, and Argentina. Along with several Interandean Valles, they are typically dominated by deciduous woodland,
shrub and <color=#3366CC>xeric</color> vegetation, reaching the extreme in the slopes near the virtually lifeless <color=#3366CC>Atacama Desert</color>.
About 30,000 species of <color=#3366CC>vascular plants</color> live in the Andes, with roughly half being <color=#3366CC>endemic</color> to the region, surpassing the
diversity of any other hotspot. The small tree Cinchona pubescens, a source of <color=#3366CC>quinine</color> that is used to treat <color=#3366CC>malaria</color>, is
found widely in the Andes as far south as Bolivia. Other important crops that originated from the Andes are <color=#3366CC>tobacco</color> and

<color=#3366CC>potatoes</color>. The high-altitude <color=#3366CC>Polylepis</color> forests and woodlands are found in the Andean areas of <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Peru</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bolivia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>. These trees, by locals referred to as Queñua, Yagual, and other names, can be found at
altitudes of 4500 m above sea level. It remains unclear if the patchy distribution of these forests and woodlands is
natural, or the result of clearing that began during the <color=#3366CC>Incan</color> period. Regardless, in <color=#3366CC>modern times</color>, the clearance has
accelerated, and the trees are now considered highly <color=#3366CC>endangered</color>, with some believing that as little as 10% of the
original <color=#3366CC>woodland</color> remains.
Fauna
The Andes are rich in fauna: With almost 1,000 species, of which roughly 2/3 are <color=#3366CC>endemic</color> to the region, the Andes are
the most important region in the world for <color=#3366CC>amphibians</color>. The diversity of animals in the Andes is high, with almost 600
species of <color=#3366CC>mammals</color> (13% endemic), more than 1,700 species of birds (about 1/3 endemic), more than 600 species of
<color=#3366CC>reptiles</color> (about 45% endemic), and almost 400 species of fish (about 1/3 endemic).

The <color=#3366CC>vicuña</color> and <color=#3366CC>guanaco</color> can be found living in the <color=#3366CC>Altiplano</color>, while the closely related <color=#3366CC>domesticated</color> <color=#3366CC>llama</color> and <color=#3366CC>alpaca</color>
are widely kept by locals as <color=#3366CC>pack animals</color> and for their <color=#3366CC>meat</color> and <color=#3366CC>wool</color>. The crepuscular (active during dawn and dusk)
<color=#3366CC>chinchillas</color>, two threatened members of the <color=#3366CC>rodent</color> order, inhabit the Andes' alpine regions. The <color=#3366CC>Andean condor</color>, the
largest bird of its kind in the <color=#3366CC>Western Hemisphere</color>, occurs throughout much of the Andes but generally in very low
densities. Other animals found in the relatively open habitats of the high Andes include the huemul, <color=#3366CC>cougar</color>, foxes in the
genus <color=#3366CC>Pseudalopex</color>, and, for birds, certain species of <color=#3366CC>tinamous</color> (notably members of the genus Nothoprocta), Andean
goose, giant coot, <color=#3366CC>flamingos</color> (mainly associated with hypersaline lakes), lesser rhea, Andean flicker, diademed
sandpiper-plover, miners, sierra-finches and diuca-finches.
<color=#3366CC>Lake Titicaca</color> hosts several endemics, among them the highly endangered Titicaca flightless grebe and Titicaca water
frog. A few species of <color=#3366CC>hummingbirds</color>, notably some hillstars, can be seen at altitudes above 4000 m, but far higher
diversities can be found at lower altitudes, especially in the humid Andean forests ("cloud forests") growing on slopes in
Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and far northwestern Argentina. These forest-types, which includes the Yungas and
parts of the Chocó, are very rich in flora and fauna, although few large mammals exist, exceptions being the threatened
mountain tapir, <color=#3366CC>spectacled bear</color>, and yellow-tailed woolly monkey.
Birds of humid Andean forests include mountain toucans, quetzals, and the Andean cock-of-the-rock, while
mixed-species flocks dominated by <color=#3366CC>tanagers</color> and <color=#3366CC>furnariids</color> are commonly seen—in contrast to several vocal but
typically cryptic species of <color=#3366CC>wrens</color>, tapaculos, and antpittas.
A number of species such as the royal cinclodes and white-browed tit-spinetail are associated with Polylepis, and
consequently also threatened.
Human activity
The Andes Mountains form a north–south axis of cultural influences. A long series of cultural development culminated
in the expansion of the <color=#3366CC>Inca civilization</color> and <color=#3366CC>Inca Empire</color> in the central Andes during the 15th century. The Incas formed
this civilization through <color=#3366CC>imperialistic</color> <color=#3366CC>militarism</color> as well as careful and meticulous governmental management. The
government sponsored the construction of <color=#3366CC>aqueducts</color> and <color=#3366CC>roads</color> in addition to pre-existing installations. Some of these
constructions still exist today.
Devastated by European diseases and by <color=#3366CC>civil war</color>, the Incas were defeated in 1532 by an alliance composed of tens of
thousands of allies from nations they had subjugated (e.g. Huancas, Chachapoyas, Cañaris) and a small army of 180
Spaniards led by <color=#3366CC>Francisco Pizarro</color>. One of the few Inca sites the Spanish never found in their conquest was <color=#3366CC>Machu</color>
<color=#3366CC>Picchu</color>, which lay hidden on a peak on the eastern edge of the Andes where they descend to the Amazon. The main
surviving languages of the Andean peoples are those of the <color=#3366CC>Quechua</color> and <color=#3366CC>Aymara language</color> families. Woodbine Parish
and Joseph Barclay Pentland surveyed a large part of the Bolivian Andes from 1826 to 1827.
Cities
In modern times, the largest cities in the Andes are <color=#3366CC>Bogotá</color>, with a metropolitan population of over ten million, and

<color=#3366CC>Santiago</color>, <color=#3366CC>Medellín</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cali</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Quito</color>. <color=#3366CC>Lima</color> is a coastal city adjacent to the Andes and is the largest city of all Andean
countries. It is the seat of the Andean Community of Nations.
<color=#3366CC>La Paz</color>, Bolivia's seat of government, is the highest capital city in the world, at an elevation of approximately 3650 m.
Parts of the La Paz conurbation, including the city of El Alto, extend up to 4200 m.

Other cities in or near the Andes include <color=#3366CC>Bariloche</color>, Catamarca, Jujuy, <color=#3366CC>Mendoza</color>, <color=#3366CC>Salta</color>, San Juan, <color=#3366CC>Tucumán</color>, and

<color=#3366CC>Ushuaia</color> in Argentina; Calama and <color=#3366CC>Rancagua</color> in Chile; <color=#3366CC>Cochabamba</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oruro</color>, <color=#3366CC>Potosí</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sucre</color>, Tarija, and Yacuiba in
Bolivia; <color=#3366CC>Arequipa</color>, Cajamarca, <color=#3366CC>Cusco</color>, Huancayo, Huánuco, Huaraz, Juliaca, and Puno in Peru; Ambato, <color=#3366CC>Cuenca</color>,
Ibarra, Latacunga, Loja, Riobamba, and Tulcán in Ecuador; Armenia, <color=#3366CC>Cúcuta</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bucaramanga</color>, Duitama, <color=#3366CC>Ibagué</color>, Ipiales,
Manizales, Palmira, <color=#3366CC>Pasto</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pereira</color>, Popayán, Rionegro, Sogamoso, Tunja, and <color=#3366CC>Villavicencio</color> in Colombia; and

<color=#3366CC>Barquisimeto</color>, La Grita, Mérida, <color=#3366CC>San Cristóbal</color>, Tovar, Trujillo, and Valera in Venezuela. The cities of <color=#3366CC>Caracas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Valencia</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Maracay</color> are in the Venezuelan Coastal Range, which is a debatable extension of the Andes at the northern
extremity of South America.
Transportation
Cities and large towns are connected with <color=#3366CC>asphalt</color>-paved roads, while smaller towns are often connected by dirt roads,
which may require a four-wheel-drive vehicle.
The rough terrain has historically put the costs of building <color=#3366CC>highways</color> and <color=#3366CC>railroads</color> that cross the Andes out of reach of
most neighboring countries, even with modern <color=#3366CC>civil engineering</color> practices. For example, the main crossover of the
Andes between Argentina and Chile is still accomplished through the Paso Internacional Los Libertadores. Only
recently have the ends of some highways that came rather close to one another from the east and the west been
connected. Much of the transportation of passengers is done via aircraft.
There is one railroad that connects Chile with Peru via the Andes, however, and there are others that make the same
connection via southern Bolivia.
There are multiple highways in Bolivia that cross the Andes. Some of these were built during a <color=#3366CC>period of war</color> between
Bolivia and <color=#3366CC>Paraguay</color>, in order to transport Bolivian troops and their supplies to the war front in the lowlands of
southeastern Bolivia and western Paraguay.
For decades, Chile claimed ownership of land on the eastern side of the Andes. These claims were given up in about
1870 during the <color=#3366CC>War of the Pacific</color> between Chile and the allied Bolivia and Peru, in a diplomatic deal to keep Peru out
of the war. The Chilean Army and Chilean Navy defeated the combined forces of Bolivia and Peru, and Chile took over
Bolivia's only province on the Pacific Coast, some land from Peru that was returned to Peru decades later. Bolivia has
been completely landlocked ever since. It mostly uses <color=#3366CC>seaports</color> in eastern Argentina and <color=#3366CC>Uruguay</color> for international
trade because its diplomatic relations with Chile have been suspended since 1978.
Because of the tortuous terrain in places, villages and towns in the mountains—to which travel via <color=#3366CC>motorized vehicles</color> is
of little use—are still located in the high Andes of Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and <color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>. Locally, the relatives of the <color=#3366CC>camel</color>,
the <color=#3366CC>llama</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>alpaca</color> continue to carry out important uses as pack animals, but this use has generally diminished in
modern times. <color=#3366CC>Donkeys</color>, <color=#3366CC>mules</color>, and horses are also useful.
Agriculture
The ancient peoples of the Andes such as the Incas have practiced <color=#3366CC>irrigation</color> techniques for over 6,000 years. Because
of the mountain slopes, terracing has been a common practice. Terracing, however, was only extensively employed
after Incan imperial expansions to fuel their expanding realm. The <color=#3366CC>potato</color> holds a very important role as an internally
consumed staple crop. <color=#3366CC>Maize</color> was also an important crop for these people, and was used for the production of chicha,

important to Andean native people. Currently, <color=#3366CC>tobacco</color>, <color=#3366CC>cotton</color>, <color=#3366CC>quinoa</color>, and <color=#3366CC>coffee</color> are the main export crops. <color=#3366CC>Coca</color>,
despite eradication programs in some countries, remains an important crop for legal local use in a mildly stimulating
<color=#3366CC>herbal tea</color>, and illegally for the production of <color=#3366CC>cocaine</color>.
Irrigation
In unirrigated land, <color=#3366CC>pasture</color> is the most common type of land use. In the rainy season (summer), part of the rangeland is
used for cropping (mainly potatoes, barley, broad beans, and wheat).
Irrigation is helpful in advancing the sowing data of the summer crops, which guarantees an early yield in periods of
food shortage. Also, by early sowing, maize can be cultivated higher up in the mountains (up to 3800 m). In addition, it
makes cropping in the dry season (winter) possible and allows the cultivation of frost-resistant vegetable crops like
<color=#3366CC>onion</color> and <color=#3366CC>carrot</color>.
Mining
The Andes rose to fame for their mineral wealth during the <color=#3366CC>Spanish conquest of South America</color>. Although Andean
Amerindian peoples crafted ceremonial jewelry of gold and other metals, the mineralizations of the Andes were first
mined on a large scale after the Spanish arrival. <color=#3366CC>Potosí</color> in present-day <color=#3366CC>Bolivia</color> and Cerro de Pasco in Peru were among
the principal mines of the Spanish Empire in the New World. <color=#3366CC>Río de la Plata</color> and <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> derive their names from the
silver of Potosí.
Currently, mining in the Andes of <color=#3366CC>Chile</color> and <color=#3366CC>Peru</color> places these countries as the first and second major producers of
<color=#3366CC>copper</color> in the world. Peru also contains the 4th-largest goldmine in the world: the Yanacocha. The Bolivian Andes
principally produce <color=#3366CC>tin</color>, although historically silver mining had a huge impact on the <color=#3366CC>economy</color> of 17th-century Europe. In
Chile in the higher portions of the Andes there are only mining districts dominated by large-scale mining, while medium
and small-scale mining is more common at lower altitudes. For mines in the high Andes there are logistical difficulties in
the use of <color=#3366CC>sea water</color>, in addition to increased probabilities of <color=#3366CC>extreme weather</color> events that may disrupt water supply.
The gold deposits of the El Indio Gold Belt tend to lie along the Argentina–Chile border and next to or below glaciers
and gold mining there have thus issues relating to the bi-nationality and their environmental impacts on glaciers.
Mining in the cold conditions in the Andes pose also difficult conditions for outdoor workers such as pallaqueras and for
the batteries of electrified machinery.
There is a long history of mining in the Andes, from the Spanish <color=#3366CC>silver</color> <color=#3366CC>mines</color> in <color=#3366CC>Potosí</color> in the 16th century to the vast
current <color=#3366CC>porphyry copper deposits</color> of Chuquicamata and Escondida in Chile and Toquepala in Peru. Other metals,
including iron, gold, and tin, in addition to non-metallic resources are important. The Andes have a vast supply of
lithium; Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile have the three largest reserves in the world respectively.

Big O notation
Big O notation is a <color=#3366CC>mathematical notation</color> that describes the approximate size of a <color=#3366CC>function</color> on a <color=#3366CC>domain</color>. Big O is a
member of a family of notations invented by the German mathematicians Paul Bachmann and Edmund Landau and
expanded by others, collectively called Bachmann–Landau notation. The letter O stands for Ordnung, that is, the order
of approximation.
In <color=#3366CC>computer science</color>, big O notation is used to <color=#3366CC>classify algorithms</color> by how their run time or space requirements grow
with the input. In <color=#3366CC>analytic number theory</color>, big O notation expresses bounds on the growth of an <color=#3366CC>arithmetical function</color>, as
for the remainder term in the <color=#3366CC>prime number theorem</color>. In <color=#3366CC>mathematical analysis</color>, including <color=#3366CC>calculus</color>, Big O notation
bounds the error when truncating a <color=#3366CC>power series</color> and expresses the quality of approximation of a real or complex
valued function by a simpler function.
Often, big O notation characterizes functions according to their growth rates as the variable becomes large: different
functions with the same <color=#3366CC>asymptotic</color> growth rate may be represented using the same O notation. The letter O is used
because the growth rate of a function is also referred to as the order of the function. A description of a function in terms
of big O notation only provides an <color=#3366CC>upper bound</color> on the growth rate of the function.
Associated with big O notation are several related notations, using the symbols, and to describe other kinds of bounds
on growth rates.
Bachmann proposed the notation in 1894 and Landau extended it in 1909. An earlier notation was proposed by Paul du
Bois-Reymond in 1870.

inspired to introduce in 1909 the notation o; hence both are now called Landau symbols. These notations were used in

his 1910 tract "Orders of Infinity", but made use of them only in three papers (1910–1913). In his nearly 400 remaining
papers and books he consistently used the Landau symbols O and o. Hardy's symbols and are not used any more.

"one-way equalities", since if the sides could be reversed, "we could deduce ridiculous things like from the identities

the equality sign is not symmetric with respect to such notations [as, in this notation,] mathematicians customarily use

For these reasons, some advocate for using set notation and write, read as " <color=#3366CC>is an element of</color> ", or " is in the set " –

The Vinogradov notations and, which are widely used in number theory

Typesetting
Big O is typeset as an italicized uppercase "O, as in the following example:. In <color=#3366CC>TeX</color>, it is produced by simply typing 'O'
inside math mode. Unlike Greek-named Bachmann–Landau notations, it needs no special symbol. However, some

The big-O originally stands for "order of" ("Ordnung", Bachmann 1894), and is thus a Latin letter. Neither Bachmann
